Sorting with a Computed Key

orderBy: { [sortBy]: order } — a property name decided at runtime, not written by hand.

Still looking at getAllTickets (Figure 3.13, previous slide): orderBy: { [sortBy]: order }. An ordinary object literal writes its property names directly — { createdAt: 'asc' } — but sortBy here is a variable, one of the four strings listTicketsQuerySchema's sortBy enum allows ('createdAt', 'updatedAt', 'subject', 'status', Figure 3.6). Square brackets around a property name in an object literal — { [sortBy]: order } — is JavaScript's computed property name syntax: it evaluates sortBy first, and uses that resulting string as the key, rather than using the literal five letters s-o-r-t-B-y.

Without it, the only way to turn a validated sortBy string into the right Prisma orderBy shape would be an if/switch naming every allowed field by hand:

// What computed keys avoid having to write:
let orderBy;
if (sortBy === 'createdAt') orderBy = { createdAt: order };
else if (sortBy === 'updatedAt') orderBy = { updatedAt: order };
else if (sortBy === 'subject') orderBy = { subject: order };
else if (sortBy === 'status') orderBy = { status: order };

{ [sortBy]: order } collapses all four branches into one expression, precisely because sortBy was already validated against exactly those four values before this line ever runs — the enum in Figure 3.6 is what makes it safe to trust sortBy as a real column name here, rather than passing whatever a client typed straight through to Prisma.
